I know -- and have unfortunately dated -- plenty of men who careen from one girlfriend directly into another, often with a big fat overlap; connecting the two relationships like a murky Venn diagram. At the very least, you will never be fully able to trust an Overlapper. Because -- as yet another cliche based in truth goes -- if he does it with you, he'll do it to you. 2. Drama! Breakups are never fun, however splits caused by infidelity are hands down the most explosive. If you're like my friend and her man (who, against all odds, actually left his wife), this means that instead of talking about hearts, flowers, and butterflies -- like other new couples -- you spend your nights plotting how to hide assets and whether or not your overpaid lawyer is enough of a shark. How romantic! 3. The Pressure! Though they may appear independent, people who can't be alone are that way because they need to see themselves reflected in someone else's adoring eyes. But when their mirror (aka, partner) develops a flaw (weight gain, job loss, etc.), their image of themselves reflects that. Being a narcissist, nothing less than perfection is acceptable, so they start looking for the next mirror. Got that, fatty? You'd better stay at the top of your game if you want to hang onto an Overlapper. 4. Not cute! "I met my boyfriend when his puppy peed on my foot" is the perfect example of a meet-cute story. It has all the key elements -- chance, humor, and, best of all, a cuddly puppy! "I met my boyfriend because I was his kids' nanny and then his wife found out, which is how I got this black eye," is definitely not a tale you're going to want to share at parties. # Understanding Overlappers: The Hidden Cost of Cheating

## What Is an Overlapper?

Overlappers are people who refuse to end one relationship until they have already secured a replacement. Rather than facing the discomfort of being single, they deliberately orchestrate a transition from one partner to the next, ensuring they never have to experience a moment alone. This calculated behavior allows them to slip seamlessly from an old relationship into a new one, treating their romantic life like a series of stepping stones.

## A Behavior That Knows No Gender

It would be a mistake to assume that only one gender engages in this practice. Both men and women can be Overlappers, and when they do, they often create a significant overlap between their old and new relationships. During this transitional period, they maintain a foothold in both connections simultaneously, keeping their current partner in the dark while they cultivate a bond with someone new.

## Why Overlapping Is a Form of Cheating

At its core, overlapping is a form of cheating. It inherently involves deception—whether toward the current partner, the new interest, or often both parties at once. The Overlapper prioritizes their own comfort and desires above honesty, manipulating the people around them to get exactly what they want. This dishonesty is not incidental to the behavior; it is the very mechanism that makes overlapping possible.

## The Inevitable Consequences

Starting a relationship built on dishonesty tends to backfire. A foundation laid with deception is fundamentally unstable, and it rarely supports a healthy, lasting connection. Perhaps more importantly, you can never fully trust an Overlapper. The logic is simple but sobering: someone who is willing to cheat *with* you has already demonstrated their willingness to cheat *on* you. The very trait that brought them into your life is the same trait that threatens to take them out of it.

## The Fallout of Infidelity

Breakups caused by infidelity are among the most explosive and dramatic of all. They are marked by betrayal, anger, and heartbreak that linger long after the relationship ends. Worse still, this turmoil poisons what should be the happy, hopeful early stages of a new relationship. Instead of enjoying the excitement of a fresh start, everyone involved is left grappling with the emotional wreckage of how the transition was handled—a shadow that can darken even the most promising new beginning.

# Overlappers: The Art of Never Being Single

## Who Are the Overlappers?

Overlappers are people who refuse to end one relationship until they have secured a replacement. Rather than face the uncertainty of being alone, they treat their romantic life like a game of monkey bars—never letting go of one handhold until they've firmly grasped the next. For the Overlapper, cheating isn't necessarily about lust or passion; it's a strategic tool, a means of transitioning seamlessly from one partner to another without ever having to experience the discomfort of solitude.

At the heart of this behavior lies a deep-seated aversion to being single. For many Overlappers, the prospect of an empty apartment, a quiet weekend, or the vulnerability of starting over feels far more terrifying than the moral compromise of betrayal. So they engineer their exits carefully, lining up the next relationship before pulling the plug on the current one. To the outside world, they may appear to have effortlessly "moved on," when in reality the overlap was deliberate all along.

## Why This Behavior Is Problematic

The trouble with the Overlapper's approach is that relationships built on deception are fundamentally compromised from the start. When a new partnership begins as a secret—as the escape hatch from a previous relationship—it carries the residue of dishonesty into what should be a fresh beginning. Trust, the foundation of any healthy connection, is eroded before the relationship has even had a chance to breathe. And a person who cheated their way *into* your life has demonstrated exactly how they might one day cheat their way *out* of it.

Beyond poisoning the new relationship, overlapping tends to produce far messier endings for the old one. Honest breakups, while painful, at least offer both parties clarity and closure. The Overlapper's method, by contrast, often results in explosive, drama-filled confrontations. When the betrayed partner discovers the truth—the timeline that doesn't add up, the new flame that materialized suspiciously fast—the sense of humiliation and anger can transform an ordinary parting into a bitter, wounding ordeal.

## The Takeaway

For all these reasons, being an Overlapper is unwise, and dating one is a risk not worth taking. Choosing this path means never developing the emotional resilience that comes from standing on your own, and it means building each new relationship on a cracked foundation. And for those on the receiving end, entangling yourself with a known Overlapper is a gamble against odds that history suggests you're unlikely to beat. In matters of the heart, the courage to be temporarily alone is almost always preferable to the cowardice of never letting go.

# The Frisky Puppy

There is nothing quite as heartwarming as watching a young dog discover the world for the very first time. The energy, the curiosity, and the boundless joy make every moment memorable, especially when that puppy is feeling particularly frisky.

When our family brought home little Biscuit, we had no idea just how much life he would bring into our quiet home. From the moment he stepped through the door, the entire atmosphere changed. He would dart from room to room, sliding across the wooden floors, tumbling over his own paws, and barking at his reflection in the mirror.

The mornings were always the liveliest. When the first rays of sunlight crept through the curtains, Biscuit would spring to life, ready to play. He would grab his favorite chew toy, shake it wildly, and then race in circles around the living room. Watching him during these frisky episodes brought endless laughter to everyone in the household.

The best part, however, came in the evenings. When the day settled down and the excitement finally faded, that same frisky puppy would curl up in someone's lap, exhausted and content. In those peaceful moments, we understood the true reward of raising a happy, healthy dog.

The lesson was simple: when you welcome a frisky companion into your life, you welcome joy, chaos, and unconditional love all at once.

# The Overlappers: Or, Why That Guy Has Never Been Single Since the Bush Administration

*In defense of the terrifying, radical act of being alone for five minutes*

Let me tell you about my friend Marcus. Not his real name, because his real name would immediately identify him, and also because he currently has a girlfriend who does not know she is Girlfriend #7 in an unbroken chain stretching back to 2011 like a horrible relationship daisy chain.

Marcus is an **Overlapper**.

You know the type. The Overlapper is the person who has never, not once, in their entire adult life, been single. Not because they're irresistible catnip to the human race, but because they treat relationships like monkey bars—you don't let go of one until your hand is firmly gripping the next. There is no gap. There is no "me time." There is no soul-searching journey of self-discovery. There is only the seamless, chilling transition from Sarah to Jessica to Whoever's Next.

## My Personal Brush With The Overlapper

I dated one. Of course I did. We all have. Let's call him Derek, because that's a good name for a man who once told me he "just knew" I was the one, three weeks into us dating, while—I would later learn—still living with his ex "as roommates."

*Roommates.*

The red flag wasn't the intensity. The red flag was the *speed*. Derek moved fast, and I mistook it for passion when it was actually just logistics. He wasn't sweeping me off my feet; he was closing escrow. When we broke up eight months later, do you know how long Derek was single?

Eleven days.

**Eleven.** I've had yogurt in my fridge longer than Derek was capable of surviving on his own. And I know it was eleven days because I'm not proud of it but I did the math on Instagram like a forensic accountant of heartbreak. New girl, new couch photos, same suspiciously enthusiastic "I've never felt this way about anyone" energy I once thought was reserved for me.

That's when I understood: I wasn't special. I was just a rung.

## Why You Should Never, Ever Date An Overlapper

For your safety, your sanity, and your Instagram feed, here are the reasons to run:

1. **You are not a partner, you are a placeholder.** The Overlapper doesn't love *you*. The Overlapper loves *not being alone*. You are simply the current occupant of a role that will absolutely be recast.

2. **They cannot be alone, which means they've never done the work.** People grow in the quiet gaps between relationships. Overlappers have never experienced a quiet gap. They are emotionally the same age they were in tenth grade, just with worse knees.

3. **The overlap goes both ways.** If they left their last relationship to be with you, statistics—and basic pattern recognition—suggest they'll leave *you* to be with someone else. You're not the exception. You're the pattern.

4. **They're weirdly great at the beginning.** Overlappers have SO much practice with the honeymoon phase because they're always in one. This is not romantic. This is a *skill they've developed through repetition,* like a bartender who can flip a bottle.

5. **You'll never get a real breakup.** You'll just get *replaced.* One day the affection quietly reroutes to someone new, and you're left standing there like a Blockbuster in a Netflix world.

6. **They mistake momentum for love.** For the Overlapper, the scariest thing in the universe isn't a bad relationship. It's an empty apartment on a Tuesday night. They will choose *anyone* over *silence,* and one day, that anyone is you.

## The Bottom Line

Being single is not a failure state. It's not a layover. It's not a humiliating gap year between the "real" relationships. It's where you figure out who you actually are when nobody's watching and nobody's texting.

Overlappers never learn this, which is why they'll keep swinging from rung to rung, terrified of the ground, insisting to each new person that *this* time it's different.

It's not different, Derek.

It's just Tuesday, and you're scared of your own couch.

*Do the world a favor. Date someone who's been single long enough to miss it. They're the ones who actually know what they're looking for—and it might just be you.*

# I Used Cheating as a Bridge Between Relationships, and Honestly? Let's Talk About It

Look, I'm not here to win any morality awards. If you came looking for a redemption arc where I sob into my pillow about the sanctity of commitment, close the tab now. This is about a pattern I noticed—in myself and in half the people I know—and the uncomfortable truth about how humans actually navigate the messy exit ramps of dying relationships.

Here are the observations, numbered for your convenience, because apparently that's how we consume self-awareness now.

## 1. The "Overlap" Is Rarely an Accident

Everyone loves to call it a "moment of weakness." Please. Weakness doesn't book a hotel room. What's actually happening is you've emotionally checked out of one relationship and you're too much of a coward to slam the door before you've located the next one. It's not passion—it's project management with worse ethics.

## 2. You're Not Falling in Love, You're Building a Lifeboat

The new person isn't the love of your life. They're a flotation device. You're drowning in a relationship you don't want to be honest about ending, and here comes someone shiny who makes you feel like a person again. Spoiler: the second you're safely on shore, that lifeboat starts looking a lot less magical.

## 3. The Cowardice Is the Point

Here's the thing nobody says out loud: cheating-as-transition is fundamentally about avoiding a hard conversation. Breaking up cleanly means sitting across from someone and watching their face fall. Cheating lets you outsource that pain, delay it, and pretend the universe just *happened* to you. Convenient.

## 4. You Tell Yourself It's "Kinder" This Way

My personal favorite lie. "I didn't want to hurt them by leaving before I was sure." Translation: "I wanted my exit strategy fully financed before I filed for emotional bankruptcy." You didn't protect anyone. You just protected yourself from an awkward Tuesday.

## 5. The New Relationship Is Built on a Fault Line

Congratulations, you've started a partnership whose origin story is "we were both okay with betraying someone." That's the foundation. Don't act shocked when trust becomes a recurring theme in your future arguments. You showed each other exactly who you are in month one.

## 6. Eventually, You Run Out of Excuses

At some point the pattern stops being a series of unfortunate coincidences and starts being a personality trait. If every relationship you've ever ended came pre-loaded with the next one, the common denominator is sitting in your chair reading this article.

---

**The actual takeaway** (because even sarcastic articles need a spine):

The reason people cheat as a transition isn't that they're uniquely evil. It's that ending things honestly requires tolerating discomfort, guilt, and temporary loneliness—and a lot of us would rather do almost anything than sit alone with ourselves for a while.

The unsexy solution is boring: leave *first*, then look. Be single for a beat. Let a relationship end on its own terms instead of murdering it with an alibi. It's harder. It's lonelier. It also means the next person doesn't have to spend the whole relationship wondering when they'll become the "before."

Anyway. Do with that what you will. I'm not your therapist—I just play one on the internet.

---

*Want me to adjust the tone (edgier, more confessional, more comedic), tighten it for a specific word count, or write a punchier headline variant?*

# Why You Should Never Date Someone Who Can't Be Single

We've all met them—the people who bounce from relationship to relationship without ever pausing for breath. They break up on Friday and have a new partner by Sunday brunch. On the surface, it might look like they're just lucky in love, or maybe irresistibly charming. But there's often something more troubling underneath: an inability to simply *be alone*.

I want to tell you about my friend—let's call her Maya—because her story taught me something important about this exact type of person.

## The Setup

Maya had been with her boyfriend, Tom, for about two years when the cracks started showing. They'd fallen into that quiet, comfortable resentment that some relationships slide into. She'd complain to me over coffee about how they had nothing in common anymore, how they barely spoke, how she felt more like a roommate than a girlfriend.

"So why don't you break up?" I asked her, more than once.

She'd wave the question away. There was always a reason. The lease wasn't up. His mom was sick. It wasn't the *right time*. Now, looking back, I recognize the real reason she never named: she couldn't stand the thought of the empty space between relationships.

## The Affair

The married neighbor—I'll call him David—lived two doors down with his wife and their young son. It started innocently enough, or so Maya framed it. Friendly chats by the mailboxes. Then longer conversations. Then texts that she'd angle her phone away from so Tom couldn't see.

By the time she confessed to me what was happening, it had been going on for months.

I remember sitting across from her, stunned, asking the obvious question: "If you're this unhappy with Tom, why not just leave him? Why *this*?"

And her answer has stayed with me for years.

"I couldn't just be by myself," she admitted. "I needed to know there was someone else first."

There it was—the whole ugly truth. She didn't want David because she loved him. She wanted him because he was a bridge. A way to get from one relationship to the next without ever having to stand on solid, single ground. And in the process, she was willing to blow up a marriage, betray Tom, and become a person she didn't recognize.

## The Fallout

It ended the way these things usually do: badly, and for everyone.

David's wife found the texts. Their marriage imploded, with a child caught in the middle. Tom found out too, and the breakup was far more painful and humiliating than an honest ending ever would have been. And David—the supposed escape hatch—wanted nothing to do with Maya once his own life was in ruins.

She ended up exactly where she'd been so afraid of ending up: alone. Except now she was alone *and* carrying the guilt of the wreckage she'd left behind.

## The Lesson

Here's what Maya's story taught me, and what I want you to take from it:

**A person who can't be single isn't actually capable of choosing you.**

Think about it. When someone can only be in a relationship because they're terrified of being alone, their partner isn't a *choice*—they're a *function*. You're not the person they can't live without. You're the person who happens to be filling a hole they refuse to sit with.

That distinction matters enormously, because it changes what you can expect from them:

**They'll stay for the wrong reasons.** Maya stayed with Tom long past the point of love, not out of loyalty, but out of fear. That's not devotion. It's dependency wearing love's clothing.

**They'll cheat before they'll be alone.** When leaving means facing solitude, the "logical" move for someone like this is to secure the next thing before ending the current one. Overlap feels safer than emptiness. This is how affairs are born—not always from passion, but from cowardice.

**They'll never learn who they are.** People who can never be single never do the difficult, essential work of figuring out who they are on their own. They never learn to self-soothe, to enjoy their own company, to discover what they actually want. And you can't build a healthy partnership with someone who has no self to bring to it.

## What to Look For Instead

The healthiest partners are the ones who have *chosen* to be with you—which means they were also fully capable of choosing not to be. They know how to be alone. They've done it. They didn't like the loneliness necessarily, but they survived it, and they know they can survive it again.

That's what makes their presence meaningful. They're not with you because they're scared. They're with you because they *want* to be.

So when you're getting to know someone new, gently ask about their history. Have they ever been single for a meaningful stretch? How did they handle it? Did their last relationship end cleanly, or did it "overlap" with the one before it? Someone who has a graveyard of overlapping relationships is telling you something important about their relationship with solitude—and, by extension, with honesty.

## The Bottom Line

Maya eventually did the work. She spent nearly two years single—really, deliberately single—after the fallout. It was, she told me later, the most important thing she ever did. She learned to sit with herself. And the relationship she's in now is the first one she's ever chosen freely, rather than clung to out of fear.

The point of her story isn't to condemn her. It's to warn you.

Never date someone who can't be single, because someone who can't be alone will never truly be *with* you. They'll only be with the idea of not being by themselves—and you deserve to be more than a shelter from someone else's loneliness.

Learn to be whole on your own. And find someone who's whole on their own too. That's the only foundation worth building on.

# The Overlapper's Guide to Ruining Everything: Why You Should Swipe Left on "Serial Monobridgers"

Let me introduce you to a special breed of dater. You know the type—they've never technically been single a day in their adult life, not because they're irresistibly lovable, but because they treat relationships like monkey bars. They never let go of one branch until their other hand has a firm grip on the next.

I call them **Serial Monobridgers**: people who refuse to be single, so they build a bridge from one relationship to the next using your body as the planks.

Here's why you should send them politely (or impolitely) on their way.

## 1. Karma Is Keeping Receipts

Ask yourself one uncomfortable question: *If they cheated to be with you, what exactly are you winning?*

You didn't earn a prize. You earned a preview. The Monobridger has demonstrated, with a signed and notarized affidavit of behavior, exactly what they'll do when your relationship hits a rough patch and someone shinier appears. You are not the exception. You are the next branch.

Karma doesn't rush, but she never misses a bridge toll.

## 2. Drama Comes Standard, No Upgrade Necessary

Dating a Monobridger means inheriting an entire emotional estate you never asked for. There's the freshly wounded ex who's texting at 2 a.m. There's the mutual friend group choosing sides. There's the "we're just talking to close things out" phone call that lasts ninety minutes behind a suspiciously closed door.

You wanted a partner. You got a season finale.

## 3. You'll Live Under a Quiet, Constant Pressure

Monobridgers don't do alone time. They can't. Being single, to them, is like being asked to hold their breath underwater—technically possible, deeply unpleasant, ends in panic.

That means the pressure is always *on you*. You're not just a partner; you're a life-support system. Leave for a weekend and watch how quickly they start "reconnecting with old friends" who are conspicuously attractive and single.

## 4. Your Origin Story Will Be Deeply Unromantic

Everyone loves a good meet-cute. Locking eyes across a bookstore. Reaching for the same last umbrella. Getting seated next to each other at a wedding.

The Monobridger meet-cute goes like this:

> *"Well, I was technically still living with someone, but we had basically broken up in my heart, and then I met you, and I knew, so I ended things three days later via text while you waited in the car."*

Try telling *that* at your anniversary dinner. Try engraving *that* on anything.

## The Bottom Line

A relationship should have a beginning, not a *transition period*. Find someone brave enough to be alone—because a person who can be happy on their own is choosing you, not clinging to you.

Let the Monobridgers build their bridges. Just make sure you're not the water underneath.

---

*Now go forth and date someone with a clean emotional carfax.*

# The Understudy Always Knows the Lines: On the People Who Cast Their Next Relationship Before Firing You From the Current One

There's a particular breed of romantic operator who cannot bear to walk through an emotional doorway without first checking that another door has been propped open, oiled, and staffed by a hopeful stranger who "really *gets* them." You know the type. You may have *dated* the type. You may—and I say this with love, or at least the closest facsimile a magazine essay can offer—*be* the type.

Let's discuss the safety-net partner: the person who cannot end a relationship until the sequel has been pre-cast, storyboarded, and greenlit for production.

## The Trapeze Artist Who Never Learned to Land

Here is the official story they tell: *I'm just not the kind of person who does well alone.* Sweet. Poignant. Almost sympathetic, until you notice it's less a confession than a job posting.

Because "not doing well alone" doesn't actually mean loneliness for these people. It means something far more interesting and slightly more sinister: they cannot experience *themselves* without an audience. Left in a quiet room with no one to reflect their charm, their wit, their carefully curated aura of Someone Who Has Their Life Together, they simply... blur. They go out of focus. And so they must always keep a fresh mirror polished and waiting in the wings.

## Yes, We're Doing the Narcissism Bit

I promised you psychology, so here it is, dressed up in its Sunday clothes.

The classic narcissistic move isn't loving yourself too much—that's a rookie misreading. It's needing *other people* to supply a self you can't generate on your own. Psychologists have a delightfully clinical term for this: **narcissistic supply**. You are not a partner. You are a battery. You are recharging a person who runs out of ego the moment the room goes dark.

The safety-net enthusiast has simply industrialized this process. Why risk a power outage during the transition between relationships? Better to have the next battery installed and running *before* you toss the depleted one. Efficient! Ruthless! The Amazon Prime of heartbreak—next-day delivery on your replacement so you never experience a single evening of unfiltered contact with your own personality.

## The Mirror That Talks Back Gets Broken

Here's the tell that separates the merely anxious from the genuinely self-obsessed: watch what happens when *you*—the current partner, the incumbent, the soon-to-be-obsolete model—develop opinions. Preferences. A bad day. A need.

A mirror is only useful when it flatters. The moment you reflect something they don't want to see—their unkindness, their restlessness, the way they've already emotionally checked into their next relationship while still using your Netflix password—you become a *bad* mirror. Cracked. Distorting. And a cracked mirror doesn't get repaired. It gets replaced, quietly, with one that hasn't yet learned to show them their flaws.

The safety net was never a safety net for the relationship. It was a safety net for their self-image. You were load-bearing, darling, and you didn't even get hazard pay.

## The Grief They Never Do

The real reason healthy people can end relationships without a pre-arranged sequel is that they're willing to *grieve*. To sit in the discomfort. To spend a few months eating cereal for dinner and rediscovering that they, in fact, exist independently of whoever last told them they were special.

The safety-netter treats this necessary grief like a scheduling conflict. They cannot afford the downtime. The self might get a good look at itself during the intermission, and that self, unwitnessed and unpraised, is a horror they will do nearly anything to avoid.

So they leap. Trapeze to trapeze. Never once falling, never once flying either—just an endless, panicked reaching for the next set of hands to hold them up.

## A Small Word in Their Defense (Then We Return to the Snark)

Fine, fine. Not everyone who fears being single is a raging narcissist. Some people are simply scared, patterned by a childhood where love felt like a resource that could run out. That's real, and it deserves a therapist, not a takedown. The difference is what they do with the fear: the growing person names it and stops using human beings as furniture. The narcissist names it *charming* and keeps shopping.

## The Moral, Since Magazines Require One

If you find yourself unable to close one chapter without another already written, ghostwritten, and cast—the question isn't *who's next.* The question is: **what are you so afraid of seeing when there's no one around to reflect you back?**

Go find out. Alone. Terrifying, I know. But there's a version of you in there that doesn't require an audience to exist—and she's been waiting, in a dark and mirrorless room, for you to finally look.

She's the only reflection that was ever going to tell you the truth.
